title: At the Fish Shop
paragraphs: The man's workday was over; it was time to go home. He left the office and headed for the bus stop. As he was passing a nearby fish shop, he thought:
— Both my daughter and my wife love fish; let me make them happy this evening—I'll buy some fish and take it home, — and he went into the shop.
He approached the seller and asked him to weigh out a kilo of fish. Then he thought a little:
— Brother, if you like, make it two kilos, — he said.
— At once, — said the fishmonger, and began to fill the pan of the scales with fish.
Just then an elderly woman in a worn coat came toward them with timid steps:
— My son, will you buy some fish for me too? — she asked the man with a look of quiet distress.
— Of course, auntie, I will, — he said, and to the seller:
— Make it four kilos: two for me, and two for the auntie, — he said.
— Auntie, the fish is sorted, but you need bread with it as well. Do you have bread? — the man turned to the old woman.
The woman seemed to have swallowed her tongue; no sound came. Then, barely able to speak:
— I haven't, my child, — she said in a weak voice.
The man hurried across the street to the bakery, bought four loaves, and came back. He gave the auntie her share of the bread:
— Auntie, is there anything else you need? — he asked.
The woman reached into her pocket, took out a medicine bottle, and, shyly:
— There is, my son, — she said. — This is my eye medicine. The last time I could buy it was two months ago; now the bottle is empty. My eyes see worse and worse; I need a new one.
The man took the bottle from her hand and set off for the pharmacy. Meanwhile the fish seller, who had been watching in amazement, brought a chair and invited the woman to sit:
— Dear auntie, sit here until that fine young man comes back.

When the man returned a little later with a new bottle of medicine and saw that the fishmonger had given the auntie a place to sit, he said in his heart «well done, merciful man,» and held out the medicine to the woman:
— Is there anything else you need, mother? — he asked.
Seeing that no answer came, he reached into his pocket, took out every last bit of money he had, and gave it to the elderly woman. She said:
— May God be pleased with you, my child, — and with a smile on her face she set off for home.

Pleased that he had done a good deed, the man was heading for the stop to catch his bus when he remembered he had not paid for the fish. With not a single coin left in his pocket, he looked at the fishmonger with guilty eyes. The fishmonger only smiled:
— Go, my brother—it's on me; take it with a clear conscience, — he said.
Giving thanks, the man turned toward the stop, but having no fare either, he had to walk home. No matter—it was about half an hour's walk; he would be there soon. He called home.
— Dad, where are you? When are you coming? — his daughter asked.
— My girl, my dear, it won't be long; I'll be there soon. Tell your mother I've bought fish; tonight we'll eat fish, — he said, and set off toward home.
Joyful at heart, he raised his hands to the sky:
— My God, thanks be to You—today You made me the doer of a good deed, — he prayed.
Because of the rain that had begun to fall he quickened his steps; and the tears from his eyes ran down his cheek and mixed with the stream of water flowing along the street.
Do not wait for a convenient moment to do good; it is not the work of great means, but of a wide heart. Even when he is poor, the open-hearted man finds the path of kindness.

title: The Grocery Shop and the Supermarket
paragraphs: In our neighborhood an elderly woman kept a grocery shop. One day a supermarket opened opposite her shop. Both began writing the prices of groceries on a board in front of their stores and hanging it up. When the supermarket put up «Butter — 70 manats,» the woman put up the notice «Butter here — 60 manats.» The next day the supermarket announced «Butter — 50 manats»; without delay the auntie refreshed her board: «Butter here — 40 manats.»
Uneasy at this, one of the neighbors spoke to the woman:
— Auntie, you'd better not compete with this supermarket. They have deep pockets; when prices fall they won't suffer, but you will go bankrupt.
Without losing her composure the woman answered:
— I don't sell butter at all... Let the people at least buy it cheap.
The person who lives by the question «Whom did I help?» rather than «What did I gain?» is of another kind. The one who gives without seeking gain is in truth the one who gains the most.

title: The Garden and the Gardener
paragraphs: The teacher addresses his students:
— Imagine that a gardener tends a garden. Have you imagined it?
— We have, — the students reply.
The teacher says in a serious voice:
— Now remember well what I am about to say: one cannot claim that the garden grows thanks to the gardener alone, yet it is also untrue to say that the garden grows entirely by itself.
It is right neither to deny another's labor nor to belittle one's own. A person grows neither wholly alone nor wholly by the grace of others.

title: The Chief Accountant and the CEO
paragraphs: The chief accountant says to the CEO:
— Suppose we spent time and money on our employees' development, and yet they left our company. What do you think would happen?
The CEO:
— Suppose we gave them neither time nor expense, and they preferred to stay and not leave the company. What would happen then?
Investment in people is not a loss. The one who counts not spending as thrift chooses tomorrow's great loss for the sake of today's small comfort.

title: We Are Rich
paragraphs: Toward the end of the fourth century, Emperor Nintoku, who sat on the throne in Japan, one day climbed a high tower and surveyed his country. Seeing not even a single plume of smoke rising, he understood that his people had fallen into poverty and that no one could cook a meal in their homes.

At once he issued a decree commanding his subjects to work only for themselves for three years. He also sent the workers of his palace home. Working for themselves and paying no tax, the people by the end of three years came into abundance.
Three years later Nintoku climbed the tower again; looking at the smoke rising on every side, he was sure that hearths were burning throughout the land, and he said joyfully to the lady beside him:
— Now we are rich!
But the empress pointed to the palace, neglected for three years—its roof leaking, its flowers withered—and asked:
— You call this richness?
Nintoku's answer has never left the memory of the Japanese across the ages:
— The poverty of our people is our poverty, and their richness is our richness.
True wealth is not in the treasury, but in the well-being of the people. A leader's greatness lies not in his rank, but in the meaning he lays upon that rank.

title: An Organization Without an Action Plan
paragraphs: An organization without an action plan is like a ship whose destination is known, yet which has no sea chart, no course of travel, and no defined duties for its crew. Such a ship may sometimes reach port by chance, through a strong captain, or thanks to fair weather. But that would be the result of accidents, not of systematic management. Lasting success is won not by chance, but by well-planned activity carried out with discipline.

Such organizations lose their members over time. For what keeps people in an organization is not ideas alone, but the hope of seeing those ideas come to life. When hope is lost, people leave; and when people leave, the organization gradually fades.
A goal shows the direction; a plan gets you there. An organization without a plan advances by chance, not by lasting success.

title: Everyone Has Work to Do
paragraphs: I am very fortunate to have had wise teachers. One of them was my literature teacher, the respected Baladadash teacher. He would say that if someone has asked something of you, or entrusted you with a task, and for any reason you have been unable to carry it out, never answer that person with phrases such as «I had so much work that I had no time; I couldn't manage it»—even if that is truly how it was. For with those words you push that person to think, «Do you suppose I have no work of my own, that I trouble you for nothing?»

Everyone has work to do. A person does not trouble you out of idleness, but because they need you. Never leave a request made of you unattended, and do not force that person to wait in silence. If you will not be able to do the work, or will have no chance to carry it out, do not stay silent. Tell them without delay; do not leave a person in uncertainty. For they place hope in you and trust you. And you, after a long time has passed, come and say «I had no time»—and with that you demolish your own reliability.
To live thinking that you are someone unreliable, someone who cannot be trusted, is a very bitter feeling.

title: Henry Ford's Choice
paragraphs: It is said that one day Henry Ford, the founder of the Ford Motor Company, invited to dinner two young friends who wished to work at his company. Both young men had graduated from the same university; they were very gifted, well-educated specialists.

Dinner was eaten; the gathering ended. As they left the restaurant Ford told one of the young men that he was hiring him, and to the other he wished success and said he could not give him work. The disappointed young man gathered all his courage and asked Ford:
— Mr. Ford, all evening we spoke neither of cars nor of engineering skill; we touched only on general subjects. Yet you offered my friend a job and denied me that chance. Why did you decide so?
Ford answered thus:

— Look, young man, there are two reasons. First: throughout the meal I watched the behavior of you both. I saw that your friend tasted the food and then added salt, while you first added salt and only then tasted it. I value those people who decide to make a change only after they have tried and weighed things carefully.

— The second reason is this: your friend treated the waiters with great courtesy, while you ignored the waiters and showed courtesy only to me. People should be treated the same way regardless of the position they hold.
A person's character shows in small acts: in deciding without weighing, and in the regard shown to those who are weak.

title: Hot Bread
paragraphs: The scent of hot, fresh bread had spread through the whole street.
An elderly man approached the baker. He had to buy hot bread for his grandson. For several days the child had been asking for fresh bread.
People had lined up to buy bread. He took his place in the queue as well.
There were not many people; the line reached him quickly.

He took small change from his pocket. If he had had more money, he would have bought two loaves. He held out the money to the baker. But the baker did not take the money from the grandfather; he gave him a package.
— Take it, uncle—enjoy it.
There were three loaves in the package.
— My son, I was going to buy one loaf.
— Take all three, uncle; you'll eat them later.
The grandfather quietly drew near the baker and whispered in his ear:
— My son, I only have money for one loaf.
The baker smiled:
— Uncle, this is a share from us. Today is Friday; every Friday we give out three hot loaves. Enjoy them.
— May God be pleased with you, my child.
— Amen!
He had barely stepped away from the baker when someone called to the grandfather:
— Uncle, hey uncle!
The grandfather turned and looked:
— Yes, my son?
— Uncle, this is my mother's zakat; if you accept it, I would be very glad.
The young man slipped an envelope into the old man's pocket.
— May God accept it, my son. May God be pleased with your mother.
As he was passing by the market a woman called to him:
— Uncle... Wait a minute, please—hold on.
The elderly man stopped and looked toward the voice. A young woman held out two full bags to him:
— Dear uncle, this Ramadan we give food to everyone who passes by; please accept it too. Come now, don't refuse us—take these bags.
— May God accept it, my daughter.
— Amen, uncle!
The elderly man reached home with difficulty, weary.
— Welcome home, father.
— Where is your mother, my girl?
— In the kitchen. She said she'll cook eggs; Orkhan loves scrambled eggs.
— Take these to your mother; my back is broken.
— Grandpa, did you buy hot bread? — the grandson spoke up.
— Yes, I've bought a great many things.
— Long live Grandpa!
— Father, this morning you had no money—not even for tea.
— God gave it, my daughter.
His wife came into the room:
— How many things you've bought, my man?
— These are gifts of charity, wife.
The man told her everything that had happened, one thing after another.
The azan was called. They broke the fast with scrambled eggs. The hot bread was just right. In the bag there had been oil and cheese as well. It went very well with the tea.
— Yes, it turned out wonderfully—thanks be to God. May God accept it. The halva was very tasty too.
His grandson rose from the table and said:
— I'm going to my room to pray a little more, — and the grandfather was surprised:
— You can do that before you sleep, my son; it's still early.

— I did it at this hour yesterday. I asked God for hot cheese and bread. Look—today it came. Now I'll go pray that He send money to have your teeth fixed. Your teeth are ruined; you chew with difficulty with these teeth.
His mother smiled:
— If only your late father could have seen these days.
— My father comes into my dreams every night and sees these things anyway. In fact it was he who told me to pray.
Suddenly the old man remembered his jacket. He went to the hook, put his hand in the pocket, and took out the envelope. In the envelope there was a large sum of money.
His eyes filled.
— What is it, my man—why are your eyes moist?
— Everything that passed through our grandson's heart, the Lord has sent, wife. Just look at this money—before the holiday we can both have our teeth fixed. Thanks be to my Lord!
The sincere prayer of a child, and the kindness of a few people of good heart, become a remedy for a family's trouble. In a society that knows how to give, no one goes hungry.

title: The Former Minister at the Seminar
paragraphs: A former minister had been invited to a seminar. When his turn came he went up to the podium with a plastic cup in his hand and began his talk. But it was clear that his mind was elsewhere. Suddenly he raised the plastic cup, looked at it, and drew a deep breath. Turning his face to the hall he said:

— Do you know what I am thinking? Last year I spoke from this very podium. The only difference was that then I was a minister. When I came here a business-class ticket had been bought for me; at the airport a limousine and escort cars were waiting for me. They took me to the hotel. I rested in a luxury room, and the next day I came here in that same limousine. A special reception had been arranged. While I waited to speak they offered me coffee in an expensive china cup. Then they seated me in a specially reserved place. But today I am not speaking before you as a minister. Yesterday I flew here on a ticket I bought with my own money.

No one met me at the airport. I went to the hotel by taxi; no one escorted me to my room. When I came here this morning they checked my badge against a list and let me in. Then I sat in the first seat I found in the hall. My heart wanted coffee; they pointed me to the coffee machine in the corridor. So I went out and filled this plastic cup you see with coffee.

The seminar participants had already begun to laugh. The former minister continued thus: «I think the coffee in last year's expensive cup was offered not to me, but to my office.» Applause broke out in the hall. As soon as the applause died he said these words:

— I want to share with you this important lesson I learned: all the praise, all the services shown you, are only for your rank, your role, or your post. None of it belongs to you. Instead of the expensive cup you used while in office, when you leave office you will be given a plastic cup—that is, what you truly deserve.
The respect shown you is often for your office, not for yourself. So do not boast of your position—when it is gone, your true worth will be seen.

title: Mercedes
paragraphs: Mercedes was not the surname of its founder, nor the name of a great car company. It was the name of the daughter of a father who was devoted to automobiles.
The father believed that his daughter's name would bring him success.
And so it was...
The car to which he gave the name «Mercedes» won victory after victory in the races it entered.
Thanks to those successes, from 1902 to this day countless Mercedes automobiles have been produced.
A father's love for his daughter turned the name Mercedes into the brand of one of the world's greatest car manufacturers.
Mrs. Mercedes, who had had two unsuccessful marriages, lived in Vienna. In 1929, at the age of thirty-nine, she died of cancer and was buried in Vienna.
A name given with love, work done with love, can change the world. A father's affection made a name eternal.

title: Why Am I Poor?
paragraphs: Once a poor man met the Buddha and asked him:
— Buddha, why am I poor?
— Because you give nothing of what you have to anyone.
— But how can I do that? I have nothing to give to others!
— You have five riches with which you could share what you have, yet you do not.
— Please explain those five riches to me.
— Very well.
1. With your face you could give others a smile, yet you do not.
2. With your eyes you could look on others with mercy and love, yet you do not.
3. With your tongue you could speak kind words to others, yet you do not.
4. With your heart you could wish others happiness, yet you do not.
5. With your hands you could do good works for others, yet you do not.
You always have something to give: a smile, a kind word, a merciful look, a helping hand. A person is rich to the measure of what they share.

title: The Credit Ledger
paragraphs: A simply dressed stranger entered the neighborhood shop. After looking a while at the seller and the counter he said:
— Brother, if I asked you for bread, tea, and eggs on credit, would you give them?

— There are those who have been taking bread without pay for three months. Truth be told, I don't believe they'll settle that debt either. But what can I do—he looks after three orphans; we mustn't leave the little ones hungry. God is great; He will provide our daily bread as well. I don't ask payment for the bread I give you either. Take it and go—enjoy it with a clear conscience. — A smile passed over the stranger's face, and he said in his heart: «It seems I've found what I was looking for.»
— How much debt is there in that credit ledger of yours?
The seller asked, a little surprised and a little annoyed:
— What do you want with it?
The visitor continued the talk calmly, in a somewhat reassuring tone:

— Look, brother, I beg you—don't get angry. I'm not so idle a man as to come here and spoil your temper and take your time. I'm going to buy that ledger of yours. Please add up all the debts in it right now and tell me.

The seller looked first at the man before him, then at the overflowing ledger. Seeing that the other was insistent, he offered no resistance; he totaled all the debts recorded in the ledger and told the man the sum. The visitor took a bundle of money from the breast pocket of his jacket, laid that amount before the seller, and said:

— Brother, may God be pleased with you. If you trust people this much, and if, thinking of God, you do not leave an orphan hungry, then you are a good man. I have paid everyone's debt. Let this be my Ramadan gift to these people. Now give me that ledger. I will take it away and bury it, and I believe that on the Day of Judgment that list will be my help. — The man took the ledger and left the shop.

When the shopkeeper counted the money before him and put it in the till, he still could not fully grasp what had happened. It was as if he had been struck dumb. He looked out through the little window of the shop. The stranger was nowhere to be seen. With iftar near, everyone was hurrying home. Just then Surayya's seven-year-old daughter—her husband had died of tuberculosis—appeared in the doorway and said shyly:

— Uncle Ahmad, Mother says to give her a loaf of bread and three eggs for iftar. When my uncle comes to us next month we'll pay. — The shopkeeper seemed to wake from a dream at the girl's words. As was his habit he reached under the counter for the ledger. He paused a moment, smiled, and said:
— Come, my girl—take eggs, and bread, and oil too. And tell your mother that uncle came—and went...
Goodness done in silence is the highest goodness. To forgive a person's debt and not leave an orphan hungry is the true wealth of the heart.

title: Baklava
paragraphs: When I was a child our material circumstances were by no means good...
My father had bought a little baklava for the house. That evening, with the tea, we ate the baklava with delight.
The next day was a holiday. Mother put in my bag for school one piece of baklava, a few olives, and a bit of bread.
I went into the classroom; in front of everyone there were all kinds of foods... I too took out of my bag what Mother had given me. The child I liked least in the class came up to me and:
— I suppose you brought this baklava for the mice?! — and began to laugh.

At that moment I sank into the ground with shame; everyone began to laugh at me. Crying, I left the school, came home, and shouted at my mother: «Why did you put only one piece of baklava for me?! In the others' bags there was a world of food, and I had only one baklava, a few olives, and a bit of bread. You disgraced me!»
At that moment Mother said in a very distressed voice: «What fell to my share of the baklava was only this, my child.»

Then I hated myself; I had not even the face left to embrace my mother. Mother had not eaten the single piece of baklava that was her share since the day before; she had kept it for me. My dear mother, my self-sacrificing mother!

I know Mother would not have been hurt by me, but I was so angry with myself that for behaving that way toward such a mother I have prayed every night since I was ten for God to forgive me... Since then the only sweet I have never put in my mouth is baklava...
To laugh at someone's poverty is among the greatest sins. Let us not forget that a mother may give up even her own share—even her last bite.

title: Pay Rent for the Water
paragraphs: A man buys a water well from a villager. When he wants to draw water from the well the seller will not allow it: «I sold you the well, not the water in the well,» he says. A dispute arises. One says this, the other that—in the end they have to go before the judge.
The judge says to the seller: «Since the water is yours, you cannot keep it in someone else's well! Either take your water and go, or pay the owner of the well rent for keeping your water there.»
The one who tries to seize a right by crooked means falls into his own trap. Justice weighs the right of both sides on the scales.

title: Do You Have Spending Money?
paragraphs: Value your parents while they are alive. Never ask, «Do you have spending money?» Go and meet all their needs as far as you are able. No one can take their place.
Value your parents while they live; meet their need not with words but with deeds. Nothing and no one can take their place.

title: The Scarf Seller
paragraphs: The freezing cold of night had wrapped the city. The ground was icy and slippery. The breath leaving my mouth seemed about to turn to ice. I tried to walk with great care so as not to fall. I drew near the door of the bus and said «thank God» that I had managed to arrive without mishap. Just then a child with scarves he was trying to sell came up to me. I had no strength to deal with him; my only care was to get on the bus a moment sooner.

The child: — Will you buy one, sister? — and held out a scarf to me. To get rid of him I said: — No, I don't want it. — Buy it, sister, buy it—you'll need it, — he said. To save myself I said: — I have no money. — Never mind, sister—you take it; I don't want money; let it be from me, — he said. — That won't do; I don't want it; I have a scarf, — I said, and threw myself onto the bus. In that moment I thought only of myself; the child meant nothing to me. I hurried toward my seat.

Before I sat down I put my hand in the pocket of my coat to take out my phone. My hand touched a packet. I took it out and looked. Seeing the packet with a scarf inside, I was very surprised. It seemed the child had slipped the packet into my pocket without my noticing.

At once I threw myself out through the bus door into the street. The scarf-selling child was in the same place, trying to sell the scarf in his hand to those boarding the bus. I approached this child who paid no heed to the cold, his nose flushed bright red, his jet-black eyes shining like stars in the dark of night, revealing white teeth with an innocent smile, about twelve or thirteen years old, dressed in a thin coat, gloveless, trying to earn money in the night cold with bare hands. I laid my hand on his shoulder and showed him the scarf: — What is this?
The child smiled and said: — It's nothing, sister; you'll need it—let it be from me.
— If you do this, how will you earn money? Aren't you pitiful in this cold? — I said.
— It's all right, sister, — he said, with eyes full of love.
I held out the money.
— No, sister, I don't want it—let it be from me, — he said again.

Yet if he had looked me in the face and said, «Sister, but you had no money—where did you find it?» I would at that moment have sunk into the ground with shame. But he was a straight, innocent, pure child, his heart unsoiled, who took everyone to be as pure as himself.
— Take this, — I said, and looked firmly into his face. Seeing my resolve he took the money and with his other hand took small change from his pocket to give me the change.
— No, I don't want it—keep the change, — I said.
— Sister, this is too much; it won't do, — he said, and hurriedly tried to separate the money; some of it fell to the ground.
— It's all right, never mind—let it be from me, — I said, smiling.
The child said with that smile that melts the ice, shyly: — Thank you, sister; may God be pleased with you.

«And thank you! Thank you too, open-hearted, contented child of my poor country!» I said in my heart, and went and sat in my place. Outside, an ice-cold air had wrapped this child's small, dear city—that city in which there are still children who remain pure in their innocence, whose trust in people is unharmed, who with their smile turn winter into spring, who try to do something and earn money and support their families.

We set off. In the dark of night that city was left behind, and that scarf-selling boy as well. With a bitterness settled in my heart I thought of those souls left homeless in this cold. Inside me various feelings I could not name welled up; something knotting in my throat cut off my breath, and my tears sought every moment a chance to run from my eyes.
And our bus wound on its way between mountains covered in pure white snow.
Sometimes the greatest generosity is shown by the person with the least means. A child's pure heart turns material poverty into richness.

title: The Weight of the Oil
paragraphs: A baker used to buy a fixed amount of butter regularly from a villager. One day he saw that the weight of the butter he received from the villager had begun to grow less day by day. He accused the villager of cheating him and complained to the qadi.

When the villager was summoned before the qadi he answered thus: «In truth I have no scales at all. In one palm I place the butter I am to sell, and in the other the one-kilo loaf I buy each day from the baker, and I measure the weight of the oil by that.»
As a person treats another, so in most cases he is repaid by the same measure. The bread you give returns to you as oil.

title: His Hand Is at Work
paragraphs: A man would buy ten eggs for ten kopecks and sell them for nine. When his acquaintances asked the purpose of this strange trade, he answered thus:
— Never mind that I make a loss; seeing that I am engaged in trade, everyone takes me for a merchant; everyone sees that my hand is at work.
To kill time in meaningless work for the sake of appearances is loss itself. Merely seeming busy brings no real benefit.
